title: Working at Redwood: Roles, Career Ladders, Benefits, Hiring & Internal Tools (Employee Resources)
author: Priya Patel
body:
Overview:

This document is a single source reference for new and current Redwood employees that explains how we work, our role and career ladder structure, key benefits and perks, the hiring and onboarding flow, and the primary internal tools you will use. It is intended for all Redwood staff (engineering, product, go-to-market, and support) and is maintained by People Ops.

1) How we work (culture & expectations)

- Redwood values: engineering-first, customer-focused, production reliability, and thoughtful iteration.
- Working model: distributed team with core overlap hours (10:00–16:00 PT) suggested for cross-team collaboration. Individual teams may adjust core hours by consensus.
- Communication norms:
  - Use Slack for real-time coordination; prefer threads for multi-turn or decision-related discussions.
  - Confluence for formal docs, runbooks, and standards.
  - GitHub for code, PRs, and design proposals.
- Meeting guidance: default to asynchronous first; only schedule synchronous meetings with a clear agenda and pre-read.

2) Roles and career ladders

Intro: We maintain clear ladders for Engineering, Product, Design, SRE, and Sales/CS to make expectations explicit and support growth and promotion planning. The following condensed ladder is the canonical reference for ICs and managers.

- Individual Contributor levels (example):
  - IC1: New hire / early career contributor. Focus: shipping tasks with guidance and learning codebase.
  - IC2: Full contributor. Focus: owns features, works independently on defined scopes.
  - IC3: Senior. Focus: leads projects end-to-end, mentors peers, defines technical approach.
  - IC4: Staff. Focus: drives cross-team initiatives, architecture, and high-impact technical strategy.
  - IC5: Principal. Focus: company-level technical leadership and long-term strategy.

- Manager ladder: M1 (Manager) → M2 (Senior Manager) → M3 (Director) → M4 (Senior Director / VP). Managers are evaluated on team outcomes, people development, and cross-functional partnering.

Promotion criteria (summary):
1. Clear evidence of impact (metrics, shipped projects, product outcomes).
2. Demonstrated ownership and scope expansion beyond current level.
3. Leadership and mentoring behaviors appropriate to level.
4. Feedback from peers and cross-functional partners.

Quick reference ladder table (text):

| Level | Scope | Impact examples | Typical time in role |
| IC1 | Task-level contributor | Small features, bug fixes | 6–18 months |
| IC2 | End-to-end feature owner | Single-feature ownership, reliable delivery | 12–36 months |
| IC3 | Cross-team technical lead | Multi-feature projects, mentoring | 24–48 months |
| IC4 | Strategic owner | Architecture and platform improvements, API standards | 36+ months |

Career planning: schedule a career conversation with your manager at least twice per year. People Ops provides a Promotion Pack template (Confluence link in Resources) including evidence checklist and peer reviewers.

3) Benefits and perks (high level)

- Health and wellness:
  - Comprehensive medical, dental, and vision plans with flexible options.
  - Wellness stipend: $300/year for fitness, mental health, or ergonomics.
- Time off:
  - Generous PTO policy (flexible) plus company holidays and a discretionary winter break.
  - Parental leave: 16 weeks primary, 8 weeks secondary (adjusted by local statutory minima).
- Financial & retirement:
  - 401(k) with company match (US) or local equivalent.
  - Equity grants for all full-time employees and a transparent refresh cadence tied to performance and tenure.
- Learning and development:
  - $2,000 annual L&D allowance for conferences, courses, and books.
  - Internal mentorship program and monthly brown-bag series.
- Office & remote support:
  - Home office stipend on hire ($1,000) and annual refresh.
  - Optional office desks at major hub locations; travel stipend for on-site days when applicable.

For full plan details, vendor contacts, and eligibility, see Benefits & Perks page (HR internal link).

4) Hiring and onboarding overview

Hiring philosophy: hire for high learning velocity, service orientation to customers, and strong engineering judgment. We blend asynchronous screening with a small number of focused interviews to reduce candidate fatigue.

High-level hiring workflow (numbered):
1. Requisition opened and approved by Hiring Manager + People Ops.
2. Role profile published (job description, expected level, interview rubric).
3. Sourcing and outreach by recruiting; initial screen (30 min) to assess fit and fundamentals.
4. Take-home or technical exercise (optional by role) with clear timeboxed expectations.
5. Onsite / loop: 4–5 interviews including hiring manager, peer engineer, system design, product/cs partner, and bar raiser.
6. Debrief and calibration: interviewer notes in Greenhouse, hiring committee review if needed.
7. Offer issued: standard comp band guidance, offer packet includes benefits summary and onboarding schedule.
8. Acceptance & pre-hire checklist: background checks, equipment provisioning, and invite to Welcome cohort.

Onboarding checklist (first 90 days — numbered):
1. Pre-boarding (week before start): equipment shipped, Slack & Google workspace access granted, tentative 30/60/90 plan shared.
2. Day 1: Welcome orientation with People Ops, security briefing, setup asks (MFA, VPN), and team lunch.
3. Week 1: Access to code repos, dev environment setup, buddy assigned, first small task/bug to ship.
4. Month 1: Deeper product and architecture orientation sessions; performance expectations review with manager.
5. Month 2: Ownership of a well-scoped feature; feedback check-in at 30 and 60 days.
6. Month 3: First performance conversation; goal-setting for next quarter.

New-hire buddy program: each new hire is assigned a buddy for the first 90 days. Buddies help with informal questions, team norms, and day-to-day orientation.

5) Internal tools & how-to guides (quick reference)

- Slack: official channels, naming conventions, and incident channel etiquette. Example channels: #platform, #infra-oncall, #product-roadmap, #announcements. Use "@here" sparingly for urgent cross-team messages.
- Confluence: canonical docs live in team spaces. Keep pages up-to-date; use templates for runbooks, PRDs, and postmortems.
- GitHub: trunk-based workflows, protected release branches, and mandatory code review by at least one peer. Use labels: "bug", "feature", "p0", "security".
- CI/CD (internal): commit-triggered builds run in our CI system. Release checklist includes smoke tests, canary windows, and runbook links.
- Observability & incident tooling: dashboards (Grafana), traces (Jaeger), logs (ELK/Cloud provider), and PagerDuty for on-call rotations. See Incident Response runbook for exact steps.
- HR tools: Greenhouse (hiring), Lattice (performance & 1:1s), Gusto / ADP (payroll depending on region).

Common quick commands / examples (CLI-style):
- Clone main repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/platform.git
- Run local dev server: ./dev/run_local.sh --env=staging
- Open observability dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/overview

6) Ownership, escalation, and contacts

- People Ops (owner): Priya Patel — people-ops@redwood.com — primary owner for handbook content.
- Benefits & payroll contact: HR Benefits Team — benefits@redwood.com.
- IT & onboarding provisioning: IT Support — it-support@redwood.com.
- Engineering onboarding: eng-devops@redwood.com.

7) Governance & update cadence

- Document owner (People Ops) is responsible for quarterly review. Major policy changes require review by Legal and Finance where applicable.
- Change log: maintain short summary of material updates at the top of the page.

- Promotion Pack and Rubrics: /confluence/company-handbook/promotion-pack
